text: 3:30 in the morning. May 31st, 2003. Murphy, North Carolina — a mountain town of about 1,600 people where, at that hour, the only thing moving is the occasional patrol car.

The officer in that car is 21 years old. His name is Jeff Postell, and he's been on the job for less than a year. He swings around behind the Save-A-Lot grocery store with his lights off, and he spots a man crouched by the dumpsters.
Postell figures it's a burglar. The man bolts, then gives up. Thin, clean-shaven, polite.
He says his name is Jerry Wilson. Homeless. Just passing through from Ohio.
It's a lie, and a pretty good one.

For five years, the man standing in that parking lot had been on the FBI's Ten Most Wanted list with a million dollars on his head. Helicopters with heat cameras had flown over these exact hills looking for him.
At one point more than 200 federal agents were working out of this corner of the state.
His real name was Eric Rudolph. And seven years earlier, after a bomb went off at the Atlanta Olympics, the FBI had spent 88 days chasing someone else.
So why was he so hard to catch? There isn't one answer. There are three, and they stack on top of each other.

For the first 88 days, the FBI was looking at the wrong man — the guard who'd helped save people that night, which is the part I honestly find hardest to read about. Then for a year and a half, the real bomber didn't have a name.
And once he finally did, he walked into a place that was built for hiding.
I'm working from court records, the FBI's own case history, a Justice Department review, and news reporting from the time. When the record is fuzzy, I'll say so.
Saturday, July 27th, 1996. The Olympics are in Atlanta, and if you didn't have tickets to anything, Centennial Olympic Park was where you went. It was free.
A little after midnight there were thousands of people packed in front of a stage, and a band called Jack Mack and the Heart Attack was playing.

Working security near the big sound and light tower is a 33-year-old named Richard Jewell. Former sheriff's deputy. Now he's a contract guard for AT&T, which is not where he wanted his career to be, but it's a job.
Shortly before one in the morning, Jewell notices a green military-style backpack under a bench near the tower. Nobody's sitting there and nobody comes back for it.

Jewell points it out to Georgia Bureau of Investigation officers. One of them calls the bomb squad, and Jewell starts helping push people back. Which is harder than it sounds — you try telling a crowd at 1 a.m. to leave a concert because of a bag.
At 12:58, a call comes into 911 from a payphone a few blocks away. A man, very calm, says there's a bomb in Centennial Park and you've got 30 minutes.
According to later reporting the dispatcher had trouble even routing the warning, because the park's address wasn't in her system. The park was brand new.
He said 30 minutes. It went off at about 1:20.

Three pipe bombs, packed with nails. Alice Hawthorne, 44, from Albany, Georgia, was killed — she'd come down with her 14-year-old daughter, Fallon, who was hurt in the blast. Over a hundred other people were injured.
A Turkish TV cameraman named Melih Uzunyol had a heart attack running to film it, and died.
Investigators said afterward that the evacuation Jewell helped start kept the numbers from being a lot worse.

For three days, Richard Jewell was a hero. He went on the Today show. Then on July 30th the Atlanta Journal-Constitution put out a special edition, and the headline said the FBI suspected the "hero" guard may have planted the bomb.

It started with a tip. Before the Olympics, Jewell had worked as a campus police officer at Piedmont College in north Georgia. After the bombing, people from the college contacted investigators with concerns about how he'd behaved there.

That tip pointed the FBI toward a theory. There have been cases where someone plants a device so they can find it and be the hero. Jewell was an ex-cop who badly wanted to be a cop again, he lived with his mom, and he'd been doing interviews all week.
Suspicion isn't evidence, though. Nothing physical tied him to the backpack, and no witness put him near it before he found it. Didn't matter.
Once his name leaked, reporters camped outside his mother's apartment, agents carried boxes of their stuff out on live TV, and Jay Leno was making jokes about him.
It wasn't only the newspaper. On NBC, Tom Brokaw reportedly told viewers the FBI probably had enough to arrest him. NBC later paid Jewell a settlement over that.
CNN settled with him too.
Jewell's mother, Bobi, eventually held her own press conference. She was crying, and she asked President Clinton directly to clear her son's name.
Picture that — a mother who'd watched agents carry her things out of her apartment on live TV, now begging the President of the United States on camera.

A Justice Department review later went through how agents handled him, and one detail from it still gets me. They brought Jewell in by telling him he'd be helping make a training video for first responders.
Then, partway through, they presented his Miranda rights as if that were part of the video too. That's specifically what the Justice Department criticized.
And the thing that should've cleared him was sitting there the whole time.
It's in the phone records. A GBI agent called the bomb squad at 12:57, right after Jewell pointed out the bag. One minute later, at 12:58, the bomber called 911 from a payphone several blocks away.

One minute. Jewell's lawyers kept coming back to that, and they were right to. For Jewell to be the caller, he'd have had to point out the bag and then get to a payphone several blocks away, through a packed park, in about sixty seconds.
The question of whether Jewell could have done it didn't need a profile. It needed a clock and a map.

On October 26th, 1996 — 88 days in — the U.S. Attorney's office sent his lawyers a letter saying he was no longer a target. Attorney General Janet Reno later said publicly she was sorry about the leak.
That's three months with the investigation's attention on the wrong man. And the real bomber wasn't finished.
January 16th, 1997. A bomb goes off at a building in Sandy Springs, north of Atlanta, where an abortion clinic has its offices. Police show up.
Firefighters, federal agents. About an hour later, while they're working the scene, a second bomb explodes in the parking lot.
That second one was for them. It was set to hit whoever came running, and several responders were hurt.

A month after that, February 21st, it's the Otherside Lounge, a lesbian bar in Atlanta. Five people injured. Police sweep the area and find a second device outside — the same trick — and the bomb squad takes care of it before it goes off.
Letters start showing up at news organizations, signed "Army of God," taking credit.
By now investigators are pretty sure it's one person. Same construction, same habits, same kind of target. What they don't have is a name, and they won't get one for almost another year.
January 29th, 1998. About 7:30 a.m., outside the New Woman All Women Health Care clinic in Birmingham, Alabama.

Robert Sanderson is a Birmingham police officer working an off-duty security shift there. According to accounts of that morning, he'd noticed something by the entrance and gone over to check it. He's killed.
A nurse, Emily Lyons, is torn up by the blast — she lost an eye and went through years of surgeries. This bomb was set off by remote control, which means whoever did it was close enough to watch.
And then something happens that hadn't happened at any of the other scenes.
When a bomb goes off, people run toward it, or they freeze. A college student nearby noticed one guy doing neither. He was walking away from it.
Not fast. Just strolling off like he'd finished an errand.
That bugged the student enough to follow him. Another witness got involved, saw the man climb into a gray Nissan pickup, and wrote down the license plate.

I want to point that out, because it's the whole story in miniature. Two years of profiles, task forces and FBI theories, and the case breaks because somebody noticed a man walking the wrong way and grabbed a pen.
The truck comes back to a 31-year-old from western North Carolina. Eric Robert Rudolph.

Rudolph was born in 1966 in Merritt Island, Florida. His dad died in 1981, and his mother moved the kids up to the mountains around Topton and Murphy, right on the edge of the Nantahala National Forest.
According to reporting from the time, the family spent part of the 1980s around a church in Missouri tied to Christian Identity, which is a white supremacist religious movement.
Rudolph went into the Army in 1987, served with the 101st Airborne at Fort Campbell, Kentucky, and was out by 1989.
Then he went home. Back to the woods.

People who knew him said the same thing over and over — he knew that forest. Hunting, camping, the old logging roads, the hollows. About a week after Birmingham, agents found his gray Nissan abandoned near Murphy.
And he was just gone. Into more than half a million acres of mountain that he knew better than anyone looking for him.
May 1998, the FBI puts him on the Ten Most Wanted list. One million dollars. He's charged for Birmingham first, and later that year for the Atlanta bombings too, Olympic park included.

The task force sets up in Andrews, a small town about 15 miles from Murphy. Imagine living there in 1998 — you go to the gas station and there are guys in FBI windbreakers buying coffee, every single day, for months.
Your neighbor probably has a theory about where he's hiding. I'd bet everybody did.
What comes next is one of the biggest manhunts the country's ever run. At the peak, more than 200 federal agents, working alongside local officers who knew the ground. Helicopters with heat cameras.
Bloodhounds. Teams walking ridgelines for weeks.
Almost nothing.
Some of that is the land. The Nantahala is steep, densely wooded country, all ravines and hollows, and Rudolph had grown up in it. The people searching mostly hadn't.
The other part was the people.
A lot of folks in that corner of the state didn't trust the federal government, and they weren't shy about it. "Run, Rudolph, Run" T-shirts were for sale. There were bumper stickers.

A restaurant reportedly put up a sign joking that Rudolph ate there. I don't want to paint the whole region with that — plenty of people there were sickened by what he'd done — but the agents felt the cold shoulder, and they said so.

July 1998, there's a real break. Rudolph approaches George Nordmann, a health food store owner he knew, looking for supplies. A few days later he comes back and takes food and Nordmann's truck, leaving money and a note behind.
The truck was later recovered. Rudolph wasn't anywhere near it. The trail went cold.
Again.

There's another detail from 1998 that I genuinely didn't believe the first time I read it. In March, Rudolph's brother Daniel set up a video camera in his garage in South Carolina and cut off his own hand with a power saw.
He said it was a message to the FBI and the media. Doctors reattached it. It got investigators exactly nowhere.

After 1999 the task force shrinks. A small team keeps going, the reward stays up, and the national news moves on. Then September 11th happens and nobody's thinking about a man in the North Carolina woods anymore.
So how do you live out there for five years?

Most of what we know comes from Rudolph himself — what he told investigators after he was caught, and what agents later dug up. Keep that in your head. He has every reason to tell this as a story about a tough guy surviving on his own.
According to those accounts, he moved between hidden camps on the slopes, some of them close enough to look down on Murphy. He reportedly ate acorns. Salamanders.
Whatever he could hunt, and whatever he could pull out of people's gardens. He stole grain and buried barrels of food to get through the winters — agents later found them.
Chris Swecker, who ran the FBI's Charlotte office, also suspected he slipped into empty vacation cabins. And at night, when the town was asleep, he'd come down and go through the trash.
Which is exactly what he was doing behind the Save-A-Lot.
Here's where it gets murky, though. When Postell found him, he didn't look like a guy who'd been eating salamanders for five years. Clean-shaven, a recent haircut, fit.
Reporters started asking right away whether somebody local had been helping him.
Maybe. But a haircut isn't an accomplice. Between the buried barrels, the stolen grain, the dumpsters and possibly those empty cabins, there are other ways to explain it.
Rudolph says no. He did it alone. Nobody was ever charged with helping him.
Me? I'm not sure. I'd be careful with anybody who tells you they know for certain either way.
Back to the parking lot.

Postell isn't thinking about the Ten Most Wanted list. He thinks he's caught a prowler. Then another officer who responded takes a long look at "Jerry Wilson" and thinks he looks an awful lot like Eric Rudolph.
Under questioning, the man finally admits it.
His real name is Eric Robert Rudolph.
No shootout. No standoff. After five years, the helicopters, the dogs and a million-dollar reward, the guy was picked up by a 21-year-old rookie who thought he'd caught a burglar.
Postell said in interviews afterward that he didn't recognize him. He was just doing his rounds.
And here's the part that gets me — where was this? Murphy. Near where they'd found his abandoned truck back in 1998.
Five years, and he hadn't gone far.
And that's the part people get wrong about this manhunt. The FBI wasn't searching the wrong place.

Investigators believed he was still in western North Carolina, and some people on the task force kept the search focused there even when others figured he'd died out there or slipped away. They were right.
They were searching the right mountains. But knowing the region where a man is hiding and finding his campsite are two very different things.

Prosecutors wanted him executed. In April 2005, Rudolph made a deal instead. He pleaded guilty to all four bombings, and to stay off death row he told investigators where he'd buried explosives in the North Carolina woods.
Agents reportedly dug up around 250 pounds of dynamite.
He put out a written statement afterward. In it, he said the point of the Olympic bomb was to "confound, anger and embarrass" the government over abortion. That was his reason.
One woman dead in a park full of people at a concert.

Across the Birmingham and Atlanta cases, he got six consecutive life sentences, plus another hundred and twenty years. No parole. He's at the federal supermax in Florence, Colorado, and he isn't coming out.
Emily Lyons, the nurse from Birmingham, was in court for it.
Richard Jewell was never charged with anything, because he never did anything except notice a backpack and get people away from it. He sued several news outlets and settled with some of them.
He went back into police work in Georgia, which is all he'd wanted in the first place.
He died in August 2007. Heart trouble. He was 44.
He did live long enough to see Rudolph plead guilty. But for the last eleven years of his life, a lot of people still half-remembered him as "the Olympic bomber guy."
What bugs me most is that it's the same mistake twice, pointed in opposite directions. In 1996 the FBI looked at a man who did everything right and saw a bomber, because he fit their profile.
Then for five years, some people in those mountains looked at a man who'd killed two people and saw a folk hero, because he fit a story they liked.

The profile didn't catch Rudolph, and neither did the reward. What caught him was a college student who saw a man walking the wrong way, a stranger with a pen, and a kid cop who pulled behind a grocery store at 3:30 in the morning.
Everybody knew roughly where he was. For five years, nobody was in the right spot at the right minute. Then one night, a rookie was.
So — do you think Eric Rudolph really made it five years out there alone? Or did somebody in those mountains help him? I go back and forth on it.
Tell me what you think in the comments.
